messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** for turning “order a burger & fries” into concrete API traffic when you have only two generic helpers at your disposal:

| # | What you do | Why it matters |
|---|-------------|----------------|
| 1 | **Search the web for a suitable ordering API** | You don’t know whether McDonald’s exposes a public REST interface – the search helper lets you locate official SDKs, documentation pages, or community wrappers. |
| 2 | **Parse the discovered API spec** | Extract base URLs, auth mechanisms, resource paths (`/cart`, `/checkout`), required headers/body schema, and any OAuth / JWT flow needed. |
| 3 | **Authenticate** | Most e‑commerce flows start with login → obtain access token or session cookie. |
| 4 | **Create a new shopping basket/cart** | `POST /v1/carts` (or similar) returns a cart id. |
| 5 | **Add menu items** | For each item (“burger”, “fries”) issue `PUT/PATCH /carts/{id}/items`. Include quantity, size, modifiers. |
| 6 | **Set delivery/pickup details** | `PATCH /carts/{id}` with address or pickup slot. |
| 7 | **Apply coupons / loyalty points** *(optional)* | Some APIs expose this step. |
| 8 | **Submit payment** | Usually a separate service – pass card/token info securely. |
| 9 | **Confirm order** | Final `GET /orders/{id}` or webhook callback confirms status. |

---

### 1️⃣ Searching for the right API

```text
search_tool("McDonalds online ordering api")
```

*Expected output:*  
- Official developer portal link  
- Public Swagger/OpenAPI JSON/YAML  
- Community GitHub repo with wrapper  

If nothing turns up, fall back to *third‑party aggregators* (e.g., DoorDash, UberEats) which often provide their own APIs.

> **Tip:** Look specifically for keywords like `"menu_items"`, `"add_to_cart"`, `"place_order"`.

---

### 2️⃣ Inspecting the specification

Assume the search returned a Swagger doc hosted at `https://api.mcdonalds.com/openapi.json`.

```python
import json, urllib.request

spec_url = "https://api.mcdonalds.com/openapi.json"
with urllib.request.urlopen(spec_url) as f:
    spec = json.load(f)

print(json.dumps(spec["paths"], indent=2))
```

From here you’ll see something like:

```json
"/sessions": { ... },
"/menus/{restaurantId}/items": { ... },
"/carts": { ... },
...
```

Pick out the sequence that matches our plan.

---

### 3️⃣ Authenticating

Most modern APIs use bearer tokens. Suppose the spec says:

```
POST /sessions/login
Body: { email, password }
Response: { token, expires_in }
```

Build the request string:

```text
requests_post(
  url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/sessions/login",
  headers={"Content-Type":"application/json"},
  params={},
  timeout=15,
  allow_redirects=True,
  stream=False,
  verify=true,
  body='{"email":"me@example.com", "password":"p@ssw0rd"}'
)
```

When executed, capture the `token`.

---

### 4️⃣ Creating a Cart

```text
requests_post(
  url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/carts",
  headers={
      "Authorization":"Bearer <TOKEN>",
      "Content-Type":"application/json"
  },
  body='{}',
  ...
)
```

Store the returned `cart_id`.

---

### 5️⃣ Adding Items

Suppose the Burger has SKU `BURGER_01` and Fries `FRIES_SMALL`.

```text
for sku, qty in [ ("BURGER_01", 1), ("FRIES_SMALL", 1) ]:
    requests_put(
        url=f"https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/carts/{cart_id}/items",
        headers={
            "Authorization":"Bearer <TOKEN>",
            "Content-Type":"application/json"
        },
        body=json.dumps({"sku":sku,"quantity":qty}),
        ...
    )
```

Check responses for success codes (200–201).

---

### 6️⃣ Setting Delivery / Pickup

```text
delivery_info = {
   "address":{"street":"123 Main St","city":"Anytown","zip":"90210"},
   "time_slot":"18:00-19:00"
}
requests_patch(
    url=f"https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/carts/{cart_id}",
    headers={"Authorization":"Bearer <TOKEN>",...},
    body=json.dumps(delivery_info),
    ...
)
```

For pickup just set `"pickup_location_id"` instead.

---

### 7️⃣ Applying Coupons (if applicable)

```text
coupon_code = "WELCOME20"

requests_post(
    url=f"https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/carts/{cart_id}/coupons",
    headers={"Authorization":"Bearer <TOKEN>"}, 
    body=json.dumps({"code": coupon_code})
)
```

Verify discount applied in subsequent cart totals.

---

### 8️⃣ Payment

Payment usually goes through a dedicated gateway. Assume:

```
POST /payments
Headers: Authorization Bearer <TOKEN>
Body: {card_token:"tok_xyz", amount_cents: total_amount}
```

Generate a secure card token beforehand (via PCI‑compliant JS library or mobile SDK). Then:

```text
payment_body = {
   "amount_cents": 1299,          # $12.99
   "currency":"USD",
   "source":"tok_xyz"
}

response = requests_post(..., body=json.dumps(payment_body))
```

On success you receive a `transaction_id`.

---

### 9️⃣ Confirm Order

Finally place the order:

```text
confirm_response = requests_post(
    url=f"https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders?cart_id={cart_id}&txn_id={transaction_id}",
    headers={"Authorization":"Bearer <TOKEN>"},
    body={}
)
```

Read the resulting `status`: `"confirmed"`, `"pending_payment"`, etc. Optionally subscribe to a webhook for real‑time updates.

---

## Putting It All Together

Here’s a compact pseudocode skeleton that ties all pieces together:

```pseudo
SEARCH_RESULT = search_web_for_api("McDonalds ordering")

SPEC_URL = SEARCH_RESULT.api_endpoint + "/openapi.json"
SPEC = fetch_json(SPEC_URL)

AUTH_TOKEN = exec_request({
    method: "POST",
    url: SPEC.paths.sessions.login.url,
    body: '{"email":"you@email.com","password":"pw"}'
}).token

CART_ID = exec_request({method:"POST", url:SPEC.paths.carts.create.url}).id

FOR EACH ITEM IN [{sku:"BURGER_01"}, {sku:"FRIES_SMALL"}]:
    exec_request({
        method:"PUT",
        url:SPEC.paths.cart.items.add.format(cart_id=CART_ID),
        body: json(item)
    })

exec_request({
    method:"PATCH",
    url:SPEC.paths.cart.update.format(cart_id=CART_ID),
    body: json(address_and_time)
})

PAYMENT_TXN = exec_request({
    method:"POST",
    url:SPEC.paths.payments.process.url,
    body: json(card_token,total)
}).txnid

ORDER_CONFIRMED = exec_request({
    method:"POST",
    url:SPEC.paths.orders.place.url,
    query:{cart_id:CART_ID, txn_id:PAYMENT_TXN}
}).status == "CONFIRMED"
```

All network interactions happen inside the `exec_request()` helper, while discovery happens once upfront with `search_web_for_api()`. Error handling, retries, logging, and compliance checks (PCI DSS, GDPR) still belong in production code but aren’t shown here because they’re orthogonal to the core idea.

---

### Caveats & Practical Notes

| Issue | Mitigation |
|-------|------------|
| No public McD API | Use partner platforms (DoorDash, Uber Eats) or build a UI automation script against the website/app. |
| Rate limits | Respect `Retry-After`; implement exponential backoff. |
| Sensitive data | Never log raw passwords or card numbers; always transmit over HTTPS. |
| Legal restrictions | Verify terms of service—automated orders might violate usage policies. |
| Multi‑factor auth | Some stores require SMS/OAuth confirmation; handle callbacks or manual input. |

With the two tools described, you now have a clear blueprint for converting a simple wish (“give me a burger & fries”) into a fully automated, end‑to‑end API transaction. Happy coding—and enjoy your meal!
